body.p: This Theatre begins to manifest a spirit of improvement, which though small enough in its outset, deserves notice and encouragement. The town have already been presented with a comedy, certainly better than usual; and this is now succeeded by a farce, which, upon the whole, may be allowed the same praise in its degree. It is called the Bee Hive, from an inn of that name on the coast, at which there happens to be a great assemblage of persons in consequence of the arrival of ships. Among others, are two Officers, (Wrench and Lovegrove) from foreign service, and a Lady and her Servant (Mrs. Mountain and Miss Kelly) who have come down, somewhat strangely, to meet a Capt. Merton, a gentleman destined for the lady by their respective parents, though hitherto unknown to her but by letter. This is one of the aforesaid Officers (Mr. Wrench), but in consequence of a feigned name which he has adopted, they meet by chance as strangers, and to their mutual delight and vexation, fall in love. After a time, the Captain discovers his mistress through her servant, and the lady herself learns from the inn-keeper that one of the strangers is named Merton. Here comes by far the best touch in the piece. The lady, confident that her lover is the person, meets him with smiles on their approach, but is thrown into consternation by being gravely introduced to his companion as the happy man. However, she soon discovers the truth, and has her full revenge by pretending to be quite satisfied; but upon seeing her lover’s despair, an explanation takes place, and the affair is happily settled.—These main circumstances are, at least, not in the common, wretched style of borrowing, which characterizes our new farces in general; and so far the author deserves praise, as well as for some turns of drollery and ludicrous comparison, not so stale as the usual routine of stage jokes. But the rest is in the old and despicable way. Capt. Merton’s friend, Rattan, who is pleasantly accused of having been "bitten by a mad adjutant," has language composed of nothing but military words and metaphors.—But the chief effect of the piece is made to depend on a favourite phrase of the innkeeper (Mathews), who talks of everything by lots,—lots of pease, lots of money, lots of satisfaction. I have often noticed the fate of this poor actor in having to represent buffoons, whose whole stock of drollery consists of nonsensical repetitions of this kind. The innkeeper gives us two songs of equal invention, written on the gabbling plan of O’Keefe and Colman, and almost equal in effect to the poetic fury of Caleb Quotem, except that Mr. Mathews has not that accomplished rapidity of utterance which distinguishes Mr. Fawcett. A few lines will afford a delicious specimen of this pithy style of writing:—

I beg the reader's pardon, but if he is not much versed in these matters, it is fit he should be informed, that such is the humour of the English stage! Oh Dilworth,—worthily called immortal, and pictured in a wreath of laurel,—how many British dramatists hast thou created by the mere force of thy monosyllabic rhymes and thy accommodating English!
